header.scope: Won: online membership billing only; front-desk processing is still with Global Payments, and phase two has no date because it depends on the partner integration.
header.tag_why: The contract sat unsigned with the controller for two weeks and was signed four days after Tobi ran a recovery analysis on Corelane's own failed renewals; the front-desk gap is what shrank the win to online only.

trigger.insight: This was a board-level churn problem, not a payments project. The evaluation began when someone reframed failed cards as lost members rather than lost transactions. The actual size of that bucket is in Maya's board deck, and we don't have it; the rep's 'a third' is a hedged guess and must not be reused as a number.
trigger.messaging: Lead with recovering involuntary churn ('members who never meant to leave') in board-reporting terms, not with payments infrastructure.

decider.insight: The rep's first answer rested on Maya saying it was her call, but the controller held the pen and sat on the paper for two weeks. Greg stayed silent for two meetings and only engaged on his own money: exit costs (he asked about termination fees twice) and a spreadsheet of his own failed renewals. The champion picked the vendor; the finance buyer decided whether anything changed, and our pitch reached him late, almost by accident.
decider.messaging: Build a finance-buyer track around the customer's own failed-payment data and the switching and exit costs, and put it in front of the controller early instead of relying on the digital champion to carry it.

competitor.insight: According to Maya, the incumbent's counter was rates plus front-desk hardware on a longer term; we never saw it. After that meeting the buying questions moved from failed payments to readers, studio-software integration and lock-in, which is ground where Global is embedded and we depend on a partner. We don't know whether Corelane accepted the terminal bundle or the longer term. If they did, phase two may already be contractually blocked.
competitor.messaging: Pre-empt the incumbent's hardware-and-lock-in counter: show the front-desk path in their studio software and address contract term and exit cost directly, instead of letting the conversation drift away from recovery.

message.insight: What landed was M10 (recovery), proved with the customer's own file. That cuts against M4's 'average uplift' and M6's independent study: their numbers moved the room, ours didn't. M1 'grow globally, in every currency' fell flat for a US and Canada gym chain. M3 'unified commerce' didn't register as a concept at all; Maya translated it to hardware.
message.messaging: For subscription businesses, replace the global opener with a recovery analysis of their own failed renewals, and drop 'unified commerce' as jargon in favour of plain front-desk language.

decided.insight: The deal went from 'keeping the incumbent honest' to signed in four days because of one artifact: a spreadsheet the controller asked to keep. We don't know what in it convinced Greg. It's also possible that limiting scope to online billing let him avoid exiting Global at the front desk. That is unverified, but it would explain why the termination-fee questions didn't block the deal.
decided.messaging: Make the customer-data recovery session a standard step before paper goes to finance, and label it as a business case for the controller, not a demo.

gaps.insight: The rep calls this a near miss, but it's the reason the win is only half a win. The front desk stayed with Global, and phase two is undated and gated on a partner we don't control. M3's claim that 'the line between them has pretty much disappeared' was exactly what we couldn't show live in their software, and the one-screen front desk is the operational line Maya cares about.
gaps.messaging: Don't claim one platform online and in-store for studio and gym verticals until we can demo the reader live inside the customer's studio software; until then, position in-store explicitly as a partner-delivered phase two.

close.rep_takeaway: Two things won this deal and both are repeatable. First, put the customer's own data in front of the person who controls the money; Greg went from silent to signing because Tobi used their file, not our average. Second, ask 'whose signature does this need?' on day one. A champion saying 'it's my call' is not the same as owning the decision. Also, drop the global opener for regional subscription businesses and start with their failed renewals.
